course.title: Operations Management
course.description: A practical introduction to operations management: how organizations transform inputs into goods and services, and how they plan, run, and improve those processes. You will cover operations strategy, process analysis, capacity and layout, quality, lean production, inventory, supply chains, forecasting, service operations, and sustainability metrics. Structure and topics are adapted from the Operations management article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Operations management is best described as...
options: managing the transformation of inputs into goods and services
questions.explanation: Operations management plans and controls the processes that turn inputs such as labor, materials, and equipment into finished goods and services.

questions.prompt: A bottleneck in a process is...
options: the step with the most workers
the step that limits the overall throughput
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is the lowest-capacity step; it caps how much the whole process can produce.

options: produce only what is needed when it is needed
questions.explanation: JIT delivers parts just as they are needed, which cuts inventory and exposes hidden problems.
EOQ finds the order size where the cost of placing orders and the cost of carrying stock are in balance.

questions.prompt: Six Sigma programs focus mainly on...
questions.explanation: Six Sigma uses data to shrink variation so that defects become very rare.

questions.prompt: In a service operation, a key difference from manufacturing is that...
options: the customer often takes part in the process
questions.explanation: Services are often produced and consumed at the same time, with the customer present and involved.

questions.prompt: Safety stock is held mainly to...
options: protect against demand and supply uncertainty
questions.explanation: Safety stock is a buffer that guards against unexpected demand spikes or supplier delays.

questions.prompt: Little's Law relates work in process, throughput, and...
questions.explanation: Little's Law states that average work in process equals throughput multiplied by average flow time.

lessons.title: What operations management is, and operations strategy
lessons.grammar_note: Inputs are what a process consumes (labor, materials, capital); outputs are the goods or services it produces. Keep the two straight when you map a process.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the operations function does, describe the transformation process at the heart of any organization, and connect everyday operations to a company's competitive strategy. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in one sentence, what does an operations function actually transform? By the end of this lesson you will be able to name the main inputs a process consumes, describe the goods or services it produces, and list the broad decisions an operations manager owns, from capacity and quality to inventory and scheduling. You will also be able to state why operations strategy must line up with the overall business strategy rather than drift off on its own. Think of operations as the engine room of the business: most of a firm's people, assets, and costs live here, which is why small improvements in operations can move the whole organization. These ideas form the backbone of every later lesson, so a clear picture now pays off again and again.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Operations management is the design and control of the processes that turn inputs into outputs. Inputs include labor, materials, equipment, energy, information, and capital. The transformation process adds value by changing the form, location, or availability of those inputs, and the output is a good, a service, or a blend of both. A bakery turns flour and labor into bread; a hospital turns staff, beds, and knowledge into care; a bank turns data and people into financial services. Every organization runs some version of this input-transformation-output model, so operations exists everywhere, not just on a factory floor. Operations strategy is the set of long-run choices about how that transformation will compete: on cost, quality, speed, flexibility, or dependability. A firm rarely leads on all of these at once, so it picks priorities and designs its processes to match. The central rule is alignment: operations decisions should support the business strategy, and the business strategy should respect what operations can realistically deliver.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: A simple way to map any operation is the input-transformation-output diagram: list the inputs on the left, the transforming process in the middle, and the outputs on the right, then mark where value is added. Managers also classify operations by the four Vs: volume (how much), variety (how many different things), variation (how much demand swings), and visibility (how much the customer sees). High volume and low variety, like a soft-drink plant, favor standardized, low-cost processes. Low volume and high variety, like a custom print shop, favor flexible processes that cost more per unit. For strategy, a common tool is the order winners and order qualifiers idea: qualifiers are the minimum traits you need just to be considered, such as a safe car, while winners are the traits that actually clinch the sale, perhaps price or styling. Example: a budget airline competes on cost and on-time dependability, so it standardizes its fleet, speeds up turnarounds, and strips optional services, and every operations choice reinforces the chosen strategy.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three parts of the basic operations model. 2) List two inputs and one output for a coffee shop. 3) Which of the four Vs is highest for a hand-made furniture maker? 4) Give one order qualifier and one order winner for a pizza delivery business. 5) Why should operations strategy align with business strategy? Answers: 1) inputs, the transformation process, and outputs. 2) inputs such as coffee beans, milk, labor, and an espresso machine; the output is a served drink and the cafe experience. 3) variety, since each piece is different and made to order. 4) a qualifier might be safe, correct food; a winner might be fast delivery or low price. 5) because operations consumes most of the firm's resources and delivers the product, so if the two are misaligned the company promises what it cannot produce, or builds strengths that customers do not value.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking operations management applies only to factories. Every organization transforms inputs into outputs, so hospitals, banks, schools, and software teams all have operations. Mistake: trying to be best at cost, quality, speed, and flexibility all at once; real operations must make trade-offs and pick priorities that fit the strategy. Mistake: treating operations strategy as a separate silo instead of a servant of the business strategy. Exit ticket: (a) In the input-transformation-output model, what sits in the middle? (b) What is the difference between an order qualifier and an order winner? Answers: (a) the transformation process, where value is added by changing the form, location, or availability of the inputs; (b) a qualifier is the minimum a product needs just to be considered by customers, while a winner is the trait that actually wins the order against competitors. Keep these distinctions sharp - they recur in every later lesson.

lessons.title: Process design and analysis
lessons.grammar_note: Throughput is a rate of output per unit of time; flow time is how long one unit spends in the process. Do not confuse a rate with a duration.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Classify a process by its layout and flow, find the bottleneck that limits output, and reason about the link between work in process, throughput, and flow time using Little's Law. Warm-up: in a line of tasks that each take a different amount of time, which one sets the pace of the whole line? By the end you will be able to sketch a process as a sequence of steps with capacities, identify the slowest step, and explain why adding work ahead of a bottleneck only grows the queue rather than the output. You will also be able to use Little's Law as a back-of-the-envelope check connecting how much work sits in a system to how fast it flows through. These analysis skills turn a vague sense that a process is slow into a precise diagnosis of where and why it is slow, which is the first step toward fixing it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Processes come in a few broad types that trade volume against variety. A project handles one large, unique output, like constructing a bridge. A job shop makes many different low-volume items, routing each through different steps. A batch process groups similar items and runs them in groups. A line or assembly flow makes high volumes of a standard product in a fixed sequence. A continuous process runs without stopping, like an oil refinery. As volume rises and variety falls, processes move from flexible and costly toward standardized and efficient. Within any process, the bottleneck is the step with the least capacity; it sets the maximum throughput of the whole system, no matter how fast the other steps run. Little's Law ties three quantities together: the average number of units in the system, called work in process or WIP, equals throughput multiplied by flow time, written conceptually as WIP = throughput x flow time. It holds for any stable process and is a powerful sanity check.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: To analyze a process, draw each step with its capacity in units per hour, then find the smallest capacity, which is the bottleneck and equals the process capacity. Example: three steps run at 60, 40, and 50 units per hour. The bottleneck is the 40-unit step, so the line can finish at most 40 units per hour even though the others are faster. Speeding up the 60-unit step changes nothing; only improving the 40-unit step raises output. Little's Law in action: suppose a clinic processes 6 patients per hour (throughput) and each patient spends on average half an hour inside (flow time = 0.5 hours). Then the average number of patients in the clinic is WIP = 6 x 0.5 = 3. Rearranged, if you observe 3 patients inside and a flow time of 0.5 hours, throughput must be 6 per hour. The same law lets you estimate how long a unit waits when you know the queue length and the service rate.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which process type fits a custom tailoring shop? 2) Steps run at 20, 35, and 25 units per hour; what is the process capacity? 3) If throughput is 10 units per hour and flow time is 2 hours, what is the average WIP? 4) Why does speeding up a non-bottleneck step not raise output? 5) A bank branch holds on average 8 customers and serves 16 per hour; what is the average flow time? Answers: 1) a job shop, since items are low-volume and varied. 2) 20 units per hour, set by the slowest step. 3) WIP = 10 x 2 = 20 units. 4) because the bottleneck still caps throughput; the faster step just waits or builds up inventory. 5) from WIP = throughput x flow time, flow time = 8 / 16 = 0.5 hours, or 30 minutes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing throughput, a rate in units per time, with flow time, a duration. Little's Law only works when the units are consistent. Mistake: trying to improve every step at once; the only step that raises output is the bottleneck, so improvement effort should start there. Mistake: adding more input ahead of a bottleneck, which simply piles up work in process and lengthens flow time without producing more. Exit ticket: (a) Define the bottleneck of a process. (b) State Little's Law and say what each term means. Answers: (a) the step with the lowest capacity, which caps the throughput of the entire process; (b) WIP = throughput x flow time, where WIP is the average number of units in the system, throughput is the output rate, and flow time is the average time a unit spends in the process. Master these three terms now; capacity planning builds directly on them.

lessons.title: Capacity planning and facility layout
lessons.grammar_note: Design capacity is the theoretical maximum; effective capacity allows for maintenance, changeovers, and breaks. Utilization compares actual output to one of these - say which.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Estimate how much a facility can produce, decide when and how to add capacity, and choose a layout that supports the chosen flow. Warm-up: if a machine could run 100 units an hour in theory but needs cleaning and setup, will you ever actually get 100? By the end you will distinguish design capacity from effective capacity, compute a simple utilization figure, and describe the main layout types and when each fits. You will also be able to explain capacity cushions and the risks of building too much or too little capacity ahead of demand. Capacity and layout are expensive, long-lived decisions, so getting the logic right matters: too little capacity turns away customers, while too much drains cash through idle assets. This lesson gives you the vocabulary and the simple arithmetic to reason about these choices before committing real money, and it connects directly to the process analysis you just learned.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Capacity is the maximum output a process can sustain. Design capacity is the ideal ceiling under perfect conditions; effective capacity is what you can realistically reach once you allow for maintenance, setups, breaks, and product mix. Actual output is usually below both. Utilization is actual output divided by design capacity, while efficiency is actual output divided by effective capacity - two different ratios, so always say which one you mean. Firms also hold a capacity cushion, which is deliberate spare capacity to absorb demand surges and uncertainty. Layout is the physical arrangement of resources. A process layout groups similar equipment together, such as all the drills in one area, and suits high variety. A product layout arranges resources in the sequence of production, as on an assembly line, and suits high volume. A fixed-position layout keeps a large product still and brings resources to it, as in shipbuilding. A cellular layout groups machines into cells that make families of similar parts, blending flexibility with flow.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Start with a simple capacity calculation: available time multiplied by the rate per machine, times the number of machines, adjusted by effective-capacity factors. Example: one line runs 8 hours a day at a design rate of 100 units per hour, giving design capacity of 800 units. If maintenance and changeovers remove 20 percent, effective capacity is about 640 units. If the line actually makes 600, utilization is 600 / 800 = 75 percent and efficiency is 600 / 640 = about 94 percent. For timing, two strategies stand out: a lead strategy adds capacity ahead of demand to avoid shortages, while a lag strategy waits until demand is proven to avoid idle assets; a match strategy adds capacity in small steps. For layout, compare a hospital, which uses a process layout because patients need different paths, with a car plant, which uses a product layout because every car follows the same line. Choosing the layout to fit volume and variety reduces travel, waiting, and wasted motion.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A machine has design capacity 500 units but effective capacity 400; actual output is 360. Compute utilization and efficiency. 2) Which layout fits a cafeteria serving a fixed meal sequence? 3) What is a capacity cushion, and why hold one? 4) Give one risk of a lead capacity strategy. 5) Which layout suits a workshop where each job takes a different route? Answers: 1) utilization = 360 / 500 = 72 percent; efficiency = 360 / 400 = 90 percent. 2) a product layout, since customers move in sequence through the same steps. 3) deliberate spare capacity kept to absorb demand surges or disruptions, so the firm does not turn customers away. 4) you may pay for idle capacity if the expected demand does not arrive. 5) a process layout, which groups similar resources and handles varied routings well.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: quoting design capacity as if it were achievable every day; real output sits below effective capacity. Mistake: mixing up utilization and efficiency - one divides by design capacity, the other by effective capacity. Mistake: running at or near 100 percent utilization and leaving no cushion, which makes the system fragile to any surge or breakdown and lengthens waiting times sharply. Mistake: choosing a layout that fights the flow, such as a rigid product layout for highly varied work. Exit ticket: (a) What is the difference between design and effective capacity? (b) Why is a capacity cushion useful? Answers: (a) design capacity is the theoretical maximum under ideal conditions, while effective capacity subtracts planned losses like maintenance and changeovers; (b) a cushion provides spare capacity to handle demand spikes and uncertainty without turning customers away or overloading the process.

questions.prompt: In the input-transformation-output model, what sits in the middle?
questions.explanation: The transformation process converts inputs into outputs by adding value.

questions.explanation: The lowest-capacity step caps the throughput of the whole process.

lessons.title: Quality management: TQM, Six Sigma, and SPC
lessons.grammar_note: Common-cause variation is the normal noise built into a stable process; special-cause variation comes from a specific, findable source. Control charts separate the two.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe what quality means in operations, explain the ideas behind total quality management and Six Sigma, and read the basic logic of statistical process control. Warm-up: if two products both meet the spec but one varies far more around the target, which process would you trust more? By the end you will be able to define quality as fitness for use and conformance to specification, outline the plan-do-check-act improvement cycle, and explain how control charts tell ordinary variation apart from signals that something has changed. You will also grasp why reducing variation, not just catching defects at the end, is the heart of modern quality thinking. These tools let a manager move from inspecting quality in after the fact to building it in from the start, which is cheaper and far more reliable. Quality underpins both cost and dependability, so it touches every other operations decision you will make.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Quality has two common meanings: fitness for use, meaning does the product do its job for the customer, and conformance to specification, meaning does it match its design targets. Total quality management, or TQM, is a company-wide approach that makes quality everyone's responsibility, driven by customer focus, continuous improvement, and data. Its engine is the plan-do-check-act (PDCA) cycle: plan a change, do it on a small scale, check the results, then act by adopting or adjusting. Six Sigma is a disciplined, data-heavy method that attacks variation; its name refers to a process so capable that defects are extremely rare, and it follows the define-measure-analyze-improve-control (DMAIC) sequence. Statistical process control (SPC) watches a process over time with control charts. A control chart plots a measurement against a center line and upper and lower control limits. Points inside the limits reflect common-cause variation, the normal noise of a stable process; points outside, or clear patterns, signal special-cause variation that has a findable source worth investigating.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: A control chart is built by sampling the process, plotting each sample, and setting control limits typically three standard deviations above and below the center line. Example: a bottler targets 500 ml per bottle. Samples hover between 495 and 505 ml, all inside the limits - this is common-cause variation, so the operator leaves the process alone. Then a sample reads 520 ml and the next reads 522 ml: points outside the upper limit signal a special cause, perhaps a stuck valve, which the team stops to fix. A key discipline is to resist tampering, because adjusting a process in response to common-cause noise actually adds variation. The cost-of-quality view sorts spending into prevention, appraisal, internal failure, and external failure costs; money spent on prevention usually saves far more in failures later. A DMAIC example: a call center defines long hold times as the problem, measures them, analyzes the causes, improves staffing and scripts, then controls the gain with ongoing charts so the fix sticks.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Give the two common definitions of quality. 2) What do the letters in PDCA stand for? 3) A control-chart point falls well above the upper control limit - common cause or special cause? 4) Why is adjusting a process in response to common-cause noise a mistake? 5) Name the four categories in the cost of quality. 6) What does the C in DMAIC ensure? Answers: 1) fitness for use and conformance to specification. 2) plan, do, check, act. 3) special cause, since it lies outside the normal variation and likely has a findable source. 4) because the noise is inherent to a stable process, so reacting to it, called tampering, adds variation rather than removing it. 5) prevention, appraisal, internal failure, and external failure costs. 6) control - it locks in the improvement with ongoing monitoring so gains do not slip back.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: relying on final inspection to achieve quality; inspection finds defects but does not prevent them, and building quality in is cheaper. Mistake: treating every wobble in a measurement as a problem - common-cause variation is normal, and reacting to it makes things worse. Mistake: confusing being within specification with being on target; a process can meet the spec yet vary so much that it is not dependable. Exit ticket: (a) What is the difference between common-cause and special-cause variation? (b) What is the goal of Six Sigma in one phrase? Answers: (a) common-cause variation is the normal, built-in noise of a stable process, while special-cause variation comes from a specific, identifiable source that has changed the process; (b) to reduce variation so sharply that defects become extremely rare.

lessons.title: Lean, just-in-time, and inventory management
lessons.grammar_note: Reorder point is a stock level that triggers an order; order quantity is how much you then order. One is a trigger, the other an amount.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the lean philosophy and the Toyota Production System, name the main forms of waste, and manage inventory with the core ideas of economic order quantity, reorder point, and safety stock. Warm-up: if holding stock ties up cash and ordering too often costs money, is there a best order size in between? By the end you will be able to describe just-in-time production and kaizen, list the classic wastes that lean tries to remove, and explain conceptually how EOQ balances ordering against holding costs. You will also be able to compute a reorder point from demand and lead time and explain why safety stock exists. Lean and inventory are two sides of one coin: lean tries to cut inventory to expose problems, while sound inventory rules keep service high without drowning in stock. This lesson ties the two together so that you can decide how much stock a firm carries and why.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Lean thinking, rooted in the Toyota Production System, aims to deliver more value with less waste. Waste, called muda in the original, is anything the customer would not pay for. The classic list has seven forms: overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, inventory, motion, and defects. Just-in-time (JIT) production makes and moves items only as they are needed, often signaled by a simple pull system called kanban, so inventory shrinks and hidden problems surface. Kaizen means continuous, incremental improvement driven by the people who do the work. Inventory management decides how much stock to hold and when to order. The economic order quantity (EOQ) is the order size that minimizes the sum of ordering cost and holding cost: order too little and you pay to reorder constantly; order too much and you pay to store it. The reorder point is the stock level at which you place a new order, set to cover expected demand during the supplier's lead time. Safety stock is extra buffer for uncertainty.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: The reorder point has a clean conceptual form: reorder point = average demand per day x lead time in days + safety stock. Example: a shop sells 50 units a day and the supplier takes 4 days, so expected demand during lead time is 50 x 4 = 200 units; add 100 units of safety stock and you reorder when stock falls to 300. EOQ balances two costs that pull in opposite directions: ordering cost falls as orders get larger and less frequent, while holding cost rises as more stock sits in the warehouse. The best order size is where the two are equal; conceptually, EOQ grows with demand and ordering cost and shrinks as holding cost rises. A lean example: a plant that switches to JIT replaces a large parts buffer with frequent small deliveries signaled by kanban cards; when a machine breaks, the thin buffer forces the problem into the open, prompting a kaizen fix rather than hiding it under a mountain of inventory.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name three of the seven wastes in lean. 2) What does a kanban signal trigger? 3) Demand is 30 units a day, lead time 5 days, safety stock 40; find the reorder point. 4) In EOQ, what two costs are being balanced? 5) Why does cutting inventory help expose problems? Answers: 1) any three of overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, inventory, motion, and defects. 2) it triggers the replenishment or production of a part only when it is needed, which is a pull system. 3) reorder point = 30 x 5 + 40 = 190 units. 4) ordering cost and holding (carrying) cost. 5) with little buffer stock, a stoppage or defect halts flow quickly and visibly, forcing the team to find and fix the root cause instead of covering it with extra stock.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating inventory as a free cushion; stock ties up cash, hides defects, and can spoil or go obsolete. Mistake: confusing the reorder point, a stock level that triggers an order, with the order quantity, which is how much you order. Mistake: setting safety stock to zero to save money, which risks stockouts whenever demand or lead time runs high. Mistake: thinking JIT means no inventory at all - it means the right amount, delivered at the right time. Exit ticket: (a) Write the conceptual reorder-point formula. (b) What is kaizen? Answers: (a) reorder point = average demand per day x lead time + safety stock; (b) kaizen is continuous, incremental improvement led by the people doing the work, a core habit of lean operations. Lean and inventory discipline work best together, not in isolation.

lessons.title: Supply chain, procurement, forecasting, and scheduling
lessons.grammar_note: A forecast is an estimate of future demand; a schedule assigns specific work to specific times and resources. Forecasts feed schedules, not the reverse.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe a supply chain and the role of procurement, explain why forecasts are needed and how they are judged, and understand the basics of scheduling work. Warm-up: why does a small swing in customer demand often cause a much larger swing in factory orders upstream? By the end you will be able to sketch the flow from suppliers through production to customers, describe what procurement does and the make-or-buy decision, and explain how forecasts are built from history and tracked for error. You will also be able to describe simple scheduling goals and sequencing rules. These topics connect the firm to the world outside its walls and to the near future: the supply chain reaches out to partners, forecasting looks ahead, and scheduling turns plans into dated, assigned work. Get these right and the whole operation runs on time and on budget.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A supply chain is the network of suppliers, producers, distributors, and retailers that moves a product from raw material to final customer, along with the flows of information and money that coordinate them. Procurement, or purchasing, is the function that selects suppliers, negotiates terms, and buys the inputs operations needs; a central choice is make-or-buy, whether to produce a part in-house or source it outside. A well-known supply-chain hazard is the bullwhip effect: small changes in end demand grow into large swings in orders upstream, because each tier reacts to its neighbor and adds its own buffer. Forecasting estimates future demand so the firm can plan. Forecasts use history, trends, and seasonality, and no forecast is perfect, so managers track forecast error to judge and improve it. Scheduling then assigns specific jobs to specific resources and times, aiming to meet due dates while keeping resources busy. Simple sequencing rules, such as first-come-first-served or shortest-processing-time-first, decide the order in which waiting jobs are run.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: A simple forecast is the moving average: average the last few periods to predict the next. Example: sales of 100, 120, and 110 over three months give a three-month moving average of (100 + 120 + 110) / 3 = 110 as next month's forecast. Forecast error is actual minus forecast; managers often track the mean absolute deviation, the average size of the errors ignoring sign, to see how far off they typically are. The bullwhip effect shows up when a retailer's modest demand rise leads a wholesaler to order more and the factory to order even more raw material, amplifying at each step; sharing real demand data up the chain dampens it. A scheduling example: three jobs wait with processing times of 2, 5, and 1 hours. Running shortest-processing-time-first, so 1, then 2, then 5, minimizes the average time jobs spend in the system, a classic result. For procurement, a make-or-buy choice weighs in-house cost and control against a supplier's lower cost or specialist skill.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the main links in a simple supply chain from raw material to customer. 2) Compute the three-period moving-average forecast from demands of 80, 90, and 100. 3) What is the bullwhip effect? 4) Jobs take 4, 1, and 3 hours; in what order does shortest-processing-time-first run them? 5) Give one factor favoring buy over make. Answers: 1) suppliers, producers (manufacturing), distributors, retailers, and the final customer. 2) (80 + 90 + 100) / 3 = 90. 3) the tendency of small changes in end-customer demand to cause progressively larger order swings upstream in the supply chain. 4) 1 hour, then 3 hours, then 4 hours. 5) a supplier can produce it more cheaply, or has specialist skills or capacity the firm lacks.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting a forecast to be exactly right; every forecast carries error, so plan for it with safety stock and by tracking the error over time. Mistake: confusing a forecast, an estimate of future demand, with a schedule, an assignment of specific work to specific times. Mistake: each tier in a chain reacting only to its immediate neighbor and hoarding buffers, which feeds the bullwhip effect; sharing real demand data calms it. Mistake: treating make-or-buy as purely a cost question and ignoring control, quality, and risk. Exit ticket: (a) What does shortest-processing-time-first scheduling minimize? (b) Why does the bullwhip effect happen? Answers: (a) it minimizes the average time jobs spend in the system, that is, average flow time; (b) because each stage reacts to its neighbor's orders and adds its own buffer, amplifying small demand changes as they move upstream.

lessons.title: Service operations and sustainability metrics
lessons.grammar_note: An input metric measures effort or resources used; an output metric measures results delivered. A good scorecard carries both.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what makes service operations distinctive, describe the customer's role in producing a service, and use common performance metrics, including sustainability measures, to judge an operation. Warm-up: can a haircut be produced today and stored for sale next week, the way a can of soup can? By the end you will be able to name the features that set services apart from goods, describe the service encounter and self-service, and read key metrics such as productivity, utilization, quality, and on-time delivery. You will also be able to explain the triple bottom line and why operations now track environmental and social performance alongside cost. Services make up most of modern economies, and sustainability pressures touch every operation, so this closing lesson connects the whole course to how real organizations measure and improve what they do. It pulls the earlier threads together into one picture of overall performance.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Services differ from goods in a few key ways, often summed up as intangibility, inseparability, variability, and perishability. A service is an experience rather than a physical object (intangible); it is often produced and consumed at the same time, with the customer present (inseparable); its quality varies with who delivers it and when (variable); and it cannot be stored for later, so an empty seat or idle hour is lost forever (perishable). Because the customer takes part in the service, choosing, describing, and sometimes self-serving, operations must design the encounter, not just the product. Performance is tracked with metrics. Productivity is output divided by input, such as units per labor hour. Other common measures include capacity utilization, quality or defect rates, on-time delivery, and cost per unit. Modern operations also weigh sustainability through the triple bottom line of people, planet, and profit, tracking energy use, emissions, waste, and safety alongside financial results, because customers, regulators, and investors increasingly demand it.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Productivity is the core efficiency metric: productivity = output / input. Example: a team produces 240 reports using 30 labor hours, so labor productivity is 240 / 30 = 8 reports per hour; raising output or trimming input lifts it. Services manage the customer's role deliberately: a buffet shifts serving work to the diner (self-service), while a fine restaurant keeps it with the staff, trading efficiency against experience. Because services are perishable, managers match capacity to demand with tools like appointments, reservations, and off-peak pricing that smooth the load. On the scorecard, a balanced view pairs input metrics such as hours and energy with output metrics such as units and satisfied customers, so no single number misleads. A sustainability example: a factory reports not only cost per unit but also kilowatt-hours per unit and waste sent to landfill, then sets targets to cut both; a delivery firm tracks fuel per parcel and plans routes to lower it. These measures turn broad goals into numbers an operation can actually manage.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four classic features that distinguish services from goods. 2) A crew makes 150 units in 25 hours; what is its labor productivity? 3) Give one way a service copes with perishability. 4) What three dimensions make up the triple bottom line? 5) Classify energy used per unit as an input or an output metric. Answers: 1) intangibility, inseparability, variability, and perishability. 2) productivity = 150 / 25 = 6 units per hour. 3) any of appointments, reservations, off-peak pricing, or flexible staffing to match capacity to demand. 4) people, planet, and profit, that is social, environmental, and economic performance. 5) an input metric, since it measures a resource consumed rather than a result delivered.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: managing a service as if it were a stockable good; a service is perishable, so unused capacity today cannot be sold tomorrow. Mistake: ignoring the customer's role, when poor instructions or clumsy self-service can wreck quality that the staff never touched. Mistake: judging an operation by a single number; productivity, quality, delivery, and sustainability can pull in different directions, so a balanced scorecard is safer. Mistake: treating sustainability as separate from operations rather than as measurable targets built into daily decisions. Exit ticket: (a) Why can most services not be inventoried? (b) What does the triple bottom line add to a cost-only view? Answers: (a) because they are perishable and usually produced and consumed at the same time, so an idle hour or empty seat is lost for good; (b) it adds social (people) and environmental (planet) performance to the financial (profit) result, giving a fuller measure of how well the operation really does.
